content: The management of menopausal symptoms has become increasingly complex since the publication of the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study, which highlighted the risks associated with hormone replacement therapy (HRT). As a result, a variety of treatment options are now available. Some women opt for prescription medications, while others turn to self-care strategies, including lifestyle changes, over-the-counter products, and complementary or alternative therapies. These therapies may include herbal remedies, exercise programs, and relaxation techniques. Relaxation techniques, which are behavioral interventions, are generally considered safe. However, their effectiveness in addressing vasomotor symptoms (such as hot flushes) and sleep disturbances remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of relaxation techniques in treating vasomotor symptoms and related sleep disturbances in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases was conducted in February 2014. These databases included the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Specialised Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, PsycINFO, Social Science Citation Index, and CINAHL. Additionally, trial registers, relevant journals, and conference abstracts were manually searched. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the review if they compared any form of relaxation intervention with either no treatment or other non-hormonal treatments for vasomotor symptoms in symptomatic perimenopausal or postmenopausal women. Two reviewers independently selected studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. When appropriate, the data from included studies were combined using a random-effects model to calculate pooled mean differences and 95% confidence intervals. Four studies, involving a total of 281 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Two studies compared relaxation techniques with electroacupuncture or superficial needling, one study compared relaxation with paced respiration or a placebo control (α-wave electroencephalographic biofeedback), and one study compared relaxation with no treatment. The results showed no evidence of a difference between relaxation techniques and acupuncture or superficial needle insertion in the number of hot flushes experienced per 24 hours (mean difference [MD] 0.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.33 to 1.43; two studies, 72 participants; I² = 0%; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, no evidence suggested a difference in hot flush severity, as measured by the Kupperman Index (MD -1.32, 95% CI -5.06 to 2.43; two studies, 72 participants; I² = 0%; very low-quality evidence). The other two studies did not provide clear evidence of a difference in hot flush frequency between relaxation techniques and paced respiration, placebo, or no treatment. However, the data from these comparisons were not suitable for statistical analysis. None of the included studies reported outcomes related to night sweats, sleep disturbances associated with night sweats, or adverse effects. The main limitations of the evidence were the small amount of available data, imprecision in the results, and insufficient reporting of study methods. In conclusion, the current evidence is insufficient to determine whether relaxation techniques are effective in treating menopausal vasomotor symptoms. Furthermore, it remains unclear whether relaxation techniques are more effective than no treatment, placebo, acupuncture, superficial needle insertion, or paced respiration.
